comments.text_zh: > 这个说法你有出处吗？关于建设成本我拿不出出处，我也承认有很多因素会让某些低密度开发项目的单位成本低于某些高密度开发项目。但建设只是事情的一部分。低密度开发会给容纳它们的城市带来糟糕的财政负担。这是因为每平方英里的应税价值低得多，而基础设施（下水道、道路等）的每英里维护和更换成本却是一样的。在许多低密度开发项目中，基础设施的维护成本往往高于该项目产生的税收收入。想了解更多关于低密度开发隐性成本的内容，我再怎么推荐 Not Just Bikes 的这个视频 [1] 都不为过。[1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: > Do you have a citation for this? I don't have a citation for construction costs, and I will concede that there are many factors that may make some low density developments cheaper per unit then some higher density development. However, construction is only part of the picture. Low density development imposes terrible financial costs for cities that contain them. That's because the taxable value per square mile is much lower, but infrastructure (sewer, roads, etc) has the same per-mile maintenance and replacement costs. The infrastructure maintenance costs in many low density developments is often greater then the amount of tax revenue the development generates. For more information on the hidden costs of low density development, I can't recommend this video [1] by Not Just Bikes enough. [1] [VIDEO]

comments.author: flaque

comments.why_zh: 概述为何低密度基础设施成本超过税收收入。
comments.quote_zh: 这里有一个很好的概述
comments.text_zh: 这个论点常被人拿来用，但在实践中根本说不通。地方越密集，基础设施的使用效率就越高。一栋公寓楼里的 50 户人家所用的管道和电线，比 50 户独栋住宅少得多。但城市获得的税收却可以是一样的。在更密集的区域，这些家庭更不太可能拥有或需要汽车，即便有，开车也更少。另一方面，低密度的郊区社区往往效率低到其基础设施的维护成本超过了居民带来的税收收入。（这里有一个很好的概述：[VIDEO]）与其说“我们没有为独栋住宅配套的基础设施”，不如说“我们没有为公寓楼配套的基础设施”更准确。
comments.text: This argument is commonly thrown around, but makes no sense in practice. The denser the place, the more efficient the infrastructure use. 50 families in a single apartment building use massively fewer pipes & power lines than 50 families in single family homes. But the tax revenue for the city can still be the same. In a denser area, those families are less likely to own or need cars, and if they do, they drive less. On the other hand, low-density suburban neighborhoods are often so inefficient that the maintenance cost of their infrastructure is more than the tax revenue the residents bring in. (Here's a good overview of that: [VIDEO] ) It's more true to say that "we don't have the infrastructure for single family homes" than it is to say that we don't have the infrastructure for apartment buildings.

comments.text_zh: 对此的一点评论是：密度较低的地区很难建设基础设施。比如说，如果有一英里长的路上住着 10 户人家，想想建一英里路要花多少钱，还要（可能）加上那里的供水和下水道。然后是每年的维护成本。再然后是为了连通这条路所需要的其他道路网络，等等。那 10 户人家交的税远远不够覆盖基础设施维护的成本。它依赖州和联邦政府的拨款，而这些钱来自密集城市的税收。我的观点是：稀疏并不客观地更好。我认为，我们在郊区和乡村地区所习以为常的生活质量，若没有密集地区带来的税收，是不可能实现的。更多信息，以及一个非常有趣的视频系列在这里：[VIDEO]
comments.text: One comment on this is that less dense areas make it very hard to build infrastructure. For example, if there are 10 families living on a mile stretch of road, think of how much it costs to build a mile of road, along with (possibly) water and sewer there. And then the annual maintenance cost. And then the other road networks require to connect that one road, etc. Those 10 families don’t pay nearly enough in taxes to cover the cost of infrastructure maintenance. It relies on grants from state and federal governments, paid for by taxes in dense cities, to cover the expense. My point: sparse is not objectively better. I think the quality of life we have come to expect in suburbs and rural areas is not possible without the taxes gained from also having dense places. More info, and a very interesting video series here: [VIDEO]

comments.text: > Those costs aren't really all that high, and are easily outweighed by the dramatically lower costs in the suburbs. Everything is cheaper there, land, buildings, repairs, goods and services. He's talking about infrastructure cost (how much it costs your municipality to provide the services that you use, like the roads) while you are talking about cost of life (how much it costs you to pay for other things that you need, like food or getting your car serviced). On the infrastructure front, suburbia simply cannot compete with cities. Infrastructure cost is bound to be more efficient where people live in more densely populated areas. The length of pipes that a municipality needs to lay down in order to serve a single family home in the suburbs is the same as a whole 6-story building in the city (the diameters of the pipes might differ). On a per-capita basis, there's no contest. A particular factor in the funding of suburban streets is that the initial paving is often subsidized by the federal government. Once the streets start crumbling down after ~20 years of usage, then the real cost hits. Here's an explanation by Not Just Bikes: [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 在美国大部分地区，这确实应该影响到独户住宅。很多城市建设郊区时靠的是一次性收费和补贴，但房子建好之后征收的税极低。事实上，税低到根本不够支付服务这些房子所需基础设施的维护费用。他们在每一栋房子上都在亏钱，还想着靠数量来弥补！他们之所以还能撑下去，唯一的原因就是高密度的城市核心区在补贴郊区。但这最终必然导致基础设施破败失修、城市破产。唯一的解决办法是提高单位土地面积的收入，也就是提高土地税，而这又意味着独户住宅的人均增税幅度要比多户住宅更大。如果你想了解更多，下面这几个 NotJustBikes 视频是这个话题的不错入门：[VIDEO] [LINK]
comments.text: In large parts of the United States it should affect single-family homes. A lot of cities constructed their suburbs with one-term fees and subsidies, but are charging extremely low taxes on the houses once constructed. In fact, the taxes are so low that they don't pay for the upkeep of the infrastructure required to service those houses. They are losing money on every house and are trying to make up for it in volume! The sole reason they have been able to continue is because the dense urban core is subsidizing the suburbs. But it'll inevitably end up with decrepit and neglected infrastructure, and cities going bankrupt. The only way to solve this is to increase the revenue per land area, which means a higher land tax, which in turn means a bigger tax increase per-person for single-family homes than for multi-family dwellings. If you want to know more, the following NotJustBikes videos are a good introduction of the subject: [VIDEO] [LINK]

comments.text_zh: 是的，但实际的计算很重要。有很多平庸的公共基础设施项目，其成本远高于它们创造的价值；也有一些理论上富有产出的公共投资，却在重复分食同一份“剩余价值”。举个例证：有很多道路是希望带动开发而修建的，结果开发从未发生，但道路照旧维护，造成可观的税收损失。再按你那样做个简单的假设：假定火车补贴创造了某种剩余价值，但接着城市又在同一条线路上同时运营公交和轮渡、还装了自行车道，而所有这些都空得令人愉快……到这一步，我们大概已经把全部剩余价值吃光了，甚至还超了。这点希望是显而易见的，然而过度修路的问题在美国无处不在，正在让我们付出巨额代价。[1] 所以我们不能只是挥挥手，断言所有基础设施和所有补贴创造的价值总是高于其成本；我们必须保持批判性，尤其要小心，不要假装非财务收益可以支付真实的财务成本。1: [VIDEO]
comments.text: Yes, but, the actual math matters. There are a lot of banal public infrastructure projects that cost much more than the value they create, and there are also theoretically productive public investments that are double-dipping into the same “surplus value.” To illustrate there are many roads that were built in hopes of spurring development and development never occurred, but the roads are maintained anyway at a substantial loss of taxes. And to make a simple hypothetical as you did, suppose the train subsidy creates some surplus, but then the city also runs a bus and a ferry and installs bike lanes all on the same route and all of these are gloriously uncrowded… at this point we’ve probably eaten up all the surplus value and then some. This is hopefully obvious, and yet the excess road building problem is ubiquitous in the US and costing us fortunes.[1] So we can’t just hand-wave and suggest that all infrastructure and all subsidies always create more value than they cost, we have to be critical and especially careful not to pretend that non-financial benefits can pay for real financial costs. 1: [VIDEO]
